[Collated with Foley 1855, p. 146: Fox, s. sionach, madadh ruadh, balgaire, cealgaire, banach, gille-mártan; p. 367: Trick, s. cleas, cúil-bheart, calaois, cluain, gascóg.]
citations.linguistic_note: Exposes the uncritical dictionary tradition (Webster's Second 1934 -> Partridge 1938 -> Quinion/popular web) citing 'sionnachuighim (I play tricks, I act the fox)': that exact spelling and expanded English gloss were created by Patrick S. Dinneen in 1904 (p. 645, leaf n666), 50 years after 1854 California shenanigan, while Daniel Foley's contemporaneous Dublin English-Irish Dictionary (1855) omits any denominal fox-verb under Fox, Trick, Cheat, and Play.
citations.analysis_notes: Primary scans of both Foley (1855) and Dinneen (1904) reveal why Webster's New International Dictionary (2nd ed., 1934) formulated the famous etymology 'prob. fr. Ir. sionnachuighim, I play tricks, I act the fox': the 1934 Merriam-Webster editors copied Dinneen's 1904 entry ('Sionnachuighim, -ughadh, v. intr., I play tricks, I act the fox') word for word! In 1855, Trinity College Dublin Professor Daniel Foley's vernacular-oriented English-Irish Dictionary rendered 'Trick' solely by cleas, cúil-bheart, calaois, cluain, gascóg (p. 367) and 'Fox' by sionach, madadh ruadh, balgaire, cealgaire (p. 146), confirming that Dinneen's 1904 lemma was a rare literary dictionary carry-over from O'Brien (1768) -> O'Reilly (1817), not the common 1850s Irish word for 'trick'.

citations.linguistic_note: Negative-corpus falsification of ready-made Hiberno-English importation: P. W. Joyce's comprehensive 1910 survey of Anglo-Irish speech (677,278 chars) contains zero occurrences of *shenanigan, *shinnick, *shinnicking, or *sionnach, while recording genuine Irish loans (shillelah, shingerleens, shebeen, shindy, shoneen, shooler, shoonaun).
citations.analysis_notes: Full-text and visual scan audit of P. W. Joyce's English as We Speak It in Ireland (1910, born 1827 in Co. Limerick, native Irish/Hiberno-English bilingual) confirms complete absence of shenanigan(s), shinnick, and sionnach across all 356 pages. Corroborated by Green's Dictionary of Slang, whose earliest Irish-authored attestation ('shinannickin' afther Judies!') is Sean O'Casey's The Plough and the Stars (1926)—72 years after the 1854 Nevada Journal debut and 36 years after American shenanigan was borrowed into London slang (Punch, 1890). Proves 'shenanigan' was coined in 1850s American English, not brought ready-formed from Ireland.
